facts.statement: The type species Isisfordia duncani was discovered in the Winton Formation in Isisford, Queensland, Australia, in the mid-1990s.
facts.quote: The type species, I. duncani. (named after the discoverer; former Deputy Mayor of Isisford, Ian Duncan) was discovered in the Winton Formation in Isisford, Queensland, Australia in the mid-1990s.

facts.statement: The initial discovery of Isisfordia included most of the animal except for the front portion of the skull.
facts.quote: Most of the animal was discovered, with the exception of the front portion of the skull.

facts.statement: A later expedition found a complete skull of Isisfordia that differed from the original specimen only in size.
facts.quote: On a later expedition to the location, paleontologists discovered a complete skull which differed from the original specimen in size only.

facts.statement: The species Isisfordia molnari was named in 2019 based on a braincase found in the Griman Creek Formation near Lightning Ridge.
facts.quote: A second species I. molnari was named in 2019 from a braincase found in the Griman Creek Formation near Lightning Ridge

facts.statement: Isisfordia lived in Australia during the Middle Cretaceous, specifically the Albian to Cenomanian stages.
facts.quote: Isisfordia is an extinct genus of crocodyliform closely related to crocodilians that lived in Australia during the Middle Cretaceous (Albian–Cenomanian).

facts.statement: Isisfordia lived between 106.3 and 93.9 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Albian to Cenomanian (106.3 to 93.9 million years ago)

facts.statement: The estimated length of Isisfordia is approximately 1.1 meters.
facts.quote: La estimación de la longitud de Isisfordia es aproximadamente 1.1 metros.

facts.statement: A 2021 study confirmed that Isisfordia is outside Eusuchia and is the sister taxon to Paralligatoridae.
facts.quote: A 2021 study by Rio and Mannion confirmed the placement of Isisfordia outside of Eusuchia, as the sister taxon to Paralligatoridae.

facts.statement: Analysis showed Isisfordia possessed vertebrae with loose ball-and-socket joints and a secondary palate similar to modern crocodilians, allowing air to pass to the lungs without entering the mouth.
facts.quote: Analysis of the remains concluded that the vertebrae fit together as they do in modern crocodilians, via loose ball-and-socket joints, as well as a secondary palate similar to that in living crocodilians which allows them to let air pass into the lungs without entering the inside of the mouth.

facts.statement: In 2020, Hart retained the species I. selaslophensis as distinct because the holotype did not overlap with specimen AM F125553.
facts.quote: Later however, Hart (2020) noted that the selaslophensis holotype didn't overlap with that of AM F125553, so he retained Etheridge's species as a distinct species, I. selaslophensis
